enrichment.short_title: Jamaican gay asylum claim and Article 8 expulsion
key_facts: Mr Dawkins, a Jamaican homosexual man, sought asylum and human rights protection against removal after entering the United Kingdom in 2000.
An adjudicator found he could practise homosexuality in Jamaica without a well-founded fear of persecution and that his relationship with H did not engage Article 8.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal refused permission to appeal, including on an out-of-time application.
The claimant concentrated his judicial review on Article 8, relying on criminalisation of homosexuality in Jamaica and past incidents of violence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for judicial review of an Immigration Appeal Tribunal refusal of permission to appeal against an adjudicator's dismissal of asylum and human rights appeals.
enrichment.outcome: Judicial review refused; permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal was granted.
enrichment.ratio: Expulsion cases engaging Convention rights outside Article 3 are fact-sensitive: mere criminalisation of homosexuality in the receiving state is insufficient, and where treatment falls short of Article 3 severity the adjudicator may lawfully find no breach of Article 8 on the facts.
legal_issues: Whether criminalisation of homosexuality alone requires asylum or human rights protection
Whether Article 8 is engaged by removal to Jamaica
Whether the adjudicator's factual findings were open
Whether the IAT lawfully refused permission to appeal
linked_authorities: Sahm Jain v Secretary of State for the Home Department

confidence.notes: Outcome, reasoning, and key authorities are explicit in the judgment. Judge metadata in the source file is empty.

enrichment.short_title: Turkish Kurd asylum claim and PKK ceasefire
key_facts: The claimant, a Turkish Kurd sympathetic to the PKK, claimed repeated detention and torture between 1996 and 2000 before claiming asylum in the United Kingdom.
The Secretary of State and adjudicator rejected much of his account of 1999 and 2000 detentions, partly because of the PKK ceasefire and withdrawal from Turkey.
The adjudicator accepted earlier detentions in 1996 and 1997 but found no real risk of persecution on return.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal refused permission to appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for judicial review of an Immigration Appeal Tribunal refusal of permission to appeal against an adjudicator's dismissal of an asylum appeal.
enrichment.ratio: An adjudicator may properly use the post-ceasefire security situation to doubt alleged PKK-related detentions and to conclude that a returned asylum seeker would not be on record or at real risk, provided reasons are adequately given.
legal_issues: Whether the adjudicator improperly relied on the PKK ceasefire
Whether the claimant would be at real risk of detention and torture on return
Whether alleged 1999 and 2000 detentions were credible
Whether the IAT erred in refusing permission to appeal

confidence.notes: Facts, findings, and outcome are clearly stated. No linked authorities are expressly relied on by name beyond generic tribunal practice.

enrichment.short_title: Introductory tenancy review letter and possession notice
key_facts: Lambeth granted Mr Forbes an introductory tenancy and later served a section 128 notice seeking possession for alleged drug-related and immoral use of the premises.
On review the council wrote that it had decided not to proceed with terminating the tenancy, but later resumed possession proceedings citing visitor noise and disturbance.
The county court adjourned possession proceedings to allow judicial review; the tenant also appealed.
The council conceded the original notice complied with section 128, but argued the original decision remained extant.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from county court possession proceedings, together with an application for judicial review of the council's decision to seek possession.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; possession refused and proceedings dismissed; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Where a review letter naturally communicates a decision not to terminate an introductory tenancy, the original decision to seek possession is reversed and later proceedings require a fresh section 128 notice setting out the reasons for the new decision.
legal_issues: Whether the review decision confirmed or reversed the decision to seek possession
Whether the original section 128 notice remained valid for later proceedings
Whether changed reasons required a further notice and review opportunity
Compatibility of the introductory tenancy scheme with Articles 6 and 8
linked_authorities: R v Bracknell Forest Borough Council ex p McLellan

confidence.notes: Statutory framework, facts, and ratio are extensively analysed in the judgment.

enrichment.short_title: Flawed credibility findings in Turkish asylum case
key_facts: The claimant, a Kurdish woman from Turkey from a politically active family, claimed repeated detention and ill-treatment before fleeing in 1999.
The adjudicator rejected her credibility mainly because she remained in Turkey after graduation despite alleged harassment and because she did not claim asylum in transit countries.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal refused leave to appeal, treating the adjudicator's reasoning as sufficient.
Collins J found the adjudicator's credibility reasoning illogical and quashed the tribunal decision.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for judicial review of an Immigration Appeal Tribunal refusal of leave to appeal against an adjudicator's dismissal of an asylum appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Claim allowed; tribunal decision quashed and remitted for reconsideration of permission to appeal.
enrichment.ratio: An adjudicator's adverse credibility finding must rest on rational reasoning; it is not lawful to reject a persecution account simply because a claimant stayed to care for a parent or failed to claim asylum while concealed in a lorry crossing Europe.
legal_issues: Whether the adjudicator's credibility findings were rational
Whether delay in leaving Turkey undermined the asylum claim
Whether failure to claim en route affected credibility
Whether the IAT lawfully upheld the adjudicator

confidence.notes: The judge's criticisms of the adjudicator's reasoning and the remittal order are explicit.

enrichment.short_title: Academic ECT challenge stayed for capable patient

statutes_considered.title: Mental Health (Hospital, Guardianship and Treatment) (England) Regulations 1983

key_facts: K, a section 3 patient with capacity, challenged planned electroconvulsive therapy by injunction.
Her responsible medical officer and trust later decided ECT was no longer necessary and revoked the section 58 second opinion certificate.
The claimant sought to amend the claim to raise general challenges to ECT, section 58, Regulation 16, and Convention rights.
Dr Hughes gave an undertaking not to administer ECT without 48 hours' notice to her solicitors unless immediately necessary to save life.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to dismiss or stay judicial review proceedings challenging proposed ECT for a detained mental health patient.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed against the second-opinion doctor; proceedings stayed generally against the RMO and trust with liberty to apply.
enrichment.ratio: Where ECT is no longer intended and the challenge has become academic, the court should not continue broad policy litigation on inadequate evidence; a general stay with liberty to apply is appropriate where interim protection remains available.
legal_issues: Whether the proceedings had become academic
Whether general ECT lawfulness issues should be determined
Whether the Salem exception justified continuing the claim
Appropriate relief where ECT was no longer proposed

confidence.notes: Procedural history, current medical position, and orders are clearly recorded. The patient is anonymised as K in the judgment.

enrichment.short_title: Pre-emption notice requiring fixed share price
key_facts: BWE International, holding 87.5% of BWE Ltd, served a transfer notice offering 275,000 shares at a base price plus net asset adjustment and a four-year bonus formula.
Mr Jones, a minority shareholder, declined the offer and refused consent to a proposed transfer to Sural CA.
The judge held the transfer notice valid; Mr Jones appealed on the construction of Article 14.2.1 alone.
By appeal hearing Sural CA had withdrawn, but costs and validity of the first notice remained in issue.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against a declaration that a pre-emption transfer notice complied with the company's articles of association.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the first transfer notice was invalid because the price was not fixed and certain at the date of the offer notice.
enrichment.ratio: Under Article 14 of a private company's pre-emption articles, a transfer notice must specify a fixed and certain price at the date of the offer notice; a formula depending on future events and deferred bonus payments does not satisfy the requirement for simultaneous completion on payment.
legal_issues: Whether a transfer notice may use a deferred or formula price
Whether price must be ascertainable at the offer notice date
How Articles 14.2.5 and 14.2.8 affect completion
Whether third-party sales must comply with the same stated price

confidence.notes: The construction issue, article wording, and Court of Appeal reasoning are detailed and explicit.

enrichment.short_title: Total loss payment discount date under bareboat charter
key_facts: A semi-submersible production platform sank on 20 March 2001 after an explosion, triggering total loss provisions in linked bareboat sale and charter contracts.
The dispute concerned whether future hire under the Loss Payment definition should be discounted to the date of total loss or to the contractual payment date 90 days later.
The difference in LIBOR movement was about US$2.5 million on a payment exceeding US$330 million.
Petromec, as upgrading contractor and assignee, pursued the preliminary issue though not a party to the bareboat contract.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of a preliminary issue on construction of Loss Payment provisions following total loss of a chartered platform.
enrichment.outcome: Loss Payment discounting held to be to 90 days after total loss; declaration made for US$334,557,499.34.
enrichment.ratio: Under clause 11.1 of the bareboat charter, future fixed hire in a Loss Payment is discounted to the date payment is declared due, meaning 90 days after total loss, not the date of the loss itself; the total loss and termination regimes in clauses 11 and 13 are distinct.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'declared due' in the Loss Payment definition
Whether discounting is to the date of total loss or date of payment
Relationship between clauses 11 and 13 regimes
Whether expert evidence on market practice was admissible

confidence.notes: Contract clauses, factual background, and declared sum are set out in detail.

enrichment.short_title: Limitation and post-accident psychiatric injury pleading
key_facts: Mr Barrow suffered a fork-lift truck accident at work in November 1995 and later developed serious psychiatric illness.
He brought a first action on liability, then sought to amend to rely on post-accident harassment and employer conduct as aggravating his condition.
A second action pleaded separate negligence after the accident; limitation and section 33 discretion arose over a three-year gap.
The county court judge invented a 'reverse mitigation' principle allowing the amendment; both actions were consolidated.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal concerning amendment of particulars and exercise of section 33 discretion in consolidated personal injury actions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on the first action amendment; cross-appeal allowed so section 33 disapplied the limitation period in the second action for different reasons than the judge.
enrichment.ratio: Post-accident breaches of duty are separate causes of action subject to limitation, not mere aggravation by reverse mitigation; where consolidated actions require examination of the same contested period, it may be equitable under section 33 to disapply limitation to avoid an unfair trial.
legal_issues: Whether post-accident employer conduct could be pleaded as aggravation without a new cause of action
Whether amendment after liability trial was permissible
Exercise of discretion under section 33 of the Limitation Act 1980
Whether prejudice arose from delay in the second action
linked_authorities: Thompson v Smiths Shiprepairers (North Shields) Ltd
Fairchild v Glenhaven Funeral Services Ltd

confidence.notes: Procedural history is complex but the Court of Appeal's rejection of the judge's principle and section 33 reasoning are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Testamentary farm option and CTO valuation timing
key_facts: The testator gave Mr Hayward an option to buy 39 acres at the price agreed with the Capital Taxes Office for inheritance tax purposes.
Executors renounced without giving notice; the residuary legatee later notified the option but no CTO valuation had been agreed by the exercise deadline.
The administratrix withdrew an agreed extension and demanded exercise before the price was known, while refusing disclosure of valuation material.
Mr Hayward sought declarations that time was not of the essence and orders for information.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part 8 claim for declarations as to exercise of a testamentary option to purchase land and disclosure of valuation information.
enrichment.outcome: Mr Hayward may wait until the price is ascertainable and then exercise within a reasonable time; disclosure order indicated in broad terms.
enrichment.ratio: Where a will grants an option at a price to be agreed with the CTO and specifies no forfeiture for late exercise, time limits in the option clause are directory rather than of the essence; Re Avard was wrongly decided.
legal_issues: Whether the three-month exercise period was mandatory
Whether the option could be exercised before the CTO price was agreed
Whether time had been made of the essence
Whether Re Avard should be followed

confidence.notes: Will clauses, factual chronology, and the judge's rejection of Re Avard are fully reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Section 2 2000 Act scope of animals in question
key_facts: Roger Baker was prosecuted for seven alleged cruelty offences relating to six ewes and one lamb.
Cornwall County Council applied under section 2 of the 2000 Act for interim care or disposal of 80 commercial animals, including 73 not identified in the informations.
The seven charged animals had already been destroyed under section 11 of the 1911 Act before the hearing.
Justices held that 'animals in question' meant only the animals to which the pending proceedings related and dismissed the application.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Prosecutor's appeal by way of case stated from magistrates' refusal of a pre-conviction section 2 application under the Protection of Animals (Amendment) Act 2000.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the justices were correct that section 2 applies only to animals to which the section 1 1911 Act proceedings relate.
enrichment.ratio: In section 2 of the Protection of Animals (Amendment) Act 2000, 'the animals in question' naturally means the animals to which the pending section 1 1911 Act proceedings relate; the interim power ends when those proceedings conclude and does not extend to other commercial animals owned by the defendant.
legal_issues: Construction of 'animals in question' in section 2(1)
Whether section 2 authorises intervention as to uncharged animals
Purpose and temporal scope of the 2000 Act interim powers
Whether Hansard was admissible under Pepper v Hart

confidence.notes: Statutory text, magistrates' findings, and Toulson J's interpretive reasoning are explicit.
